analysis.one_liner: Orders a government study of hospital contract clauses that block insurers from steering patients to cheaper care or disclosing prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2025 with no cosponsors and was referred to two House committees, where it has sat without any action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Government Accountability Office, working with the FTC and the Justice Department's antitrust division, to study four kinds of contract clauses hospitals and health systems put into deals with insurers: anti-steering clauses, anti-tiering clauses, all-or-nothing clauses, and gag clauses. These clauses stop insurers from pointing patients toward cheaper providers, stop them from setting up plans that cost less at certain hospitals, force insurers to take every hospital in a big system, and hide prices and discounts. The study would look at how these clauses affect hospital consolidation, what consumers pay for care, and whether the FTC and DOJ have the resources to enforce antitrust law against them, then send recommendations to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be patients and employers paying health premiums: a documented record of how hospital contract clauses raise prices could lay the groundwork for actual restrictions. Insurers locked into these contracts, and antitrust enforcers seeking more resources, would also gain a factual record supporting their position.

how_it_helps.text: It directs the GAO to study the effects of anti-steering, anti-tiering, all-or-nothing, and gag clauses on industry consolidation, prices consumers pay, and access to care.

It requires a public accounting of every action the FTC and DOJ have taken on these clauses and an assessment of whether those agencies have the resources to enforce antitrust law against them, plus recommendations for fixes.

analysis.who_pays: No one pays, since the bill has no direct cost beyond the study itself. If its findings led to future restrictions, large hospital systems that profit from these clauses would bear the cost of losing pricing leverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large hospital systems, if future action follows

drawbacks.text: The bill only commissions a study and a report; it does not ban any clause or change any rule, so patients would see no direct benefit even if enacted.
The study is due 18 months after enactment, meaning any follow-up legislation would likely come years after the problem was already documented.
As a single-cosponsor bill with no committee action, it may simply function as a statement of concern rather than a step toward a remedy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is minimal — a study with no binding effect, plus the risk it substitutes for real action. The potential benefit is that if the GAO confirms these clauses raise prices, Congress and the FTC would have an official factual record to act on. But a study bill with a single sponsor and no cosponsors is a modest tool, and any actual fix would still require future legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, and neither has taken it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill on April 24, 2025.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred that day to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees; no hearing, markup, or vote has followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital systems and insurers that benefit from these contract clauses are better off, since nothing has moved toward restricting them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers using restrictive clauses

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was referred to two committees.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern has formed.

industries.industry: Large hospital systems and provider groups
industries.note: The bill targets the contract clauses these systems use to keep prices high and block insurers from steering patients to cheaper options. A future ban would cut into that leverage, though this bill only studies it.

Insurers also use some of these clauses, and gag clauses can keep negotiated rates hidden. But insurers generally benefit from being able to steer patients to cheaper providers, so the study's aim aligns partly with their interest.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcers (FTC and DOJ Antitrust Division)
industries.note: The bill scrutinizes their record and their capacity, but it also asks for recommendations to give them more resources if needed.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a single sponsor and no cosponsors that are referred to multiple committees almost never get a hearing, markup, or floor vote. Unless the bill picks up cosponsors and committee attention, it will likely die quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027.
